1.pericope_label: The church at Antioch sets apart Barnabas and Saul

schools.summary: Calvin treats Paul's appointment as the key that opened the kingdom to the Gentiles, breaking the wall that Peter's errand to Cornelius had only breached by exception; he attacks the use of the word for 'ministered' to support the mass, and reads the public fast as praying not for guidance but for strength equal to the burden. Gill denies the fast fell on a sabbath and guesses it was appointed for the famine.

Lightfoot merges prophets and teachers, since Antioch was not yet mature enough for teachers without the gift of prophecy, argues that the sending out was done by the church's own settled ministers rather than visitors from Jerusalem, and refuses to build anything on the Jewish weekly fasts; with Clarke he notes that three ordainers match synagogue rule while the laying-on of hands departs from it. Henry makes the men prophets by occasional inspiration and teachers by settled office at once.

Clarke explains the ministering as the public work of prayer and service, distinguishes the divine call and qualification from the church's sanction, and details the rabbinic rule that ordination used no imposition of hands. Wesley denies flatly that this was ordination, Paul having been ordained long before and not by man, and notes that Manaen was now freed from the temptations of a court.

Robertson marks the passage as the hinge of the book, dividing the five men three and two by the Greek particles, deriving 'liturgy' from the verb, and observing that Antioch gave goodwill but no money. Ellicott distinguishes prophecy from teaching by directness of message, connects the verb with priestly ministry, and rejects the identification of Lucius with the evangelist. Barnes merges the two orders and insists the separating designates rather than ordains.
Cyril cites the verse in a catechetical proof that the Holy Spirit is a living person, since he is here seen separating, calling and sending forth with authority.

debates: Whether the prophets and teachers are two distinct orders (Robertson, dividing the five three and two; Ellicott, by the directness of the message) or one body under two names (Barnes, Lightfoot, Henry)
Whether Symeon Niger is Simon of Cyrene who carried the cross (Robertson) or a different man distinguished from him by the epithet (Ellicott)

What the laying-on of hands effected: a designation to one enterprise and nothing more (Barnes, Wesley, Robertson), or the church's formal attestation and blessing of a divine mission (Ellicott, Clarke, Calvin)
outliers: Robertson notes that the sending church contributed goodwill but no money, so the missionaries paid their own way, Philippi being the first church to support Paul financially
Lightfoot warns against three successive conjectures about the fast, each bolder than the last, and declines all of them

4.pericope_label: Sent by the Spirit to Cyprus, and preaching first in the synagogues

schools.summary: Calvin notes that no church election is mentioned because the calling was wholly divine, defends the apostles against the charge of beginning amiss by preaching to Jews when sent to Gentiles, and insists that John's ministry was help in preaching rather than bodily service. Gill explains the clause about the Spirit as a guard against supposing a merely human commission, and fills in the antiquities of Salamis.

Henry makes the Spirit's sending the ground of their courage, so that they fear no colours and leave a quiet harbour for a stormy sea, and suggests Cyprus was chosen because Barnabas was a native and would give his own country the firstfruits. Lightfoot identifies Seleucia of Pieria from Strabo, Ptolemy and Pliny, and gauges the Jewish population of Cyprus from the later revolt under Trajan.

Clarke divides the sending into influence, authority and direction, without any one of which they could not have gone at all, and keeps John Mark to minor offices so that the apostles might give themselves wholly to the doctrine. Wesley notes only that they used every opportunity offered.

Robertson observes that Luke credits the Spirit rather than the church with their authority, calls preaching to the Jew first Paul's settled rule, and takes John's title in its literal sense of under-rower, probably the synagogue attendant. Ellicott argues for a fresh revelation directing the route, supplies the history and cults of Seleucia and Cyprus, and calls Mark the courier of the apostolic church. Barnes makes him a travelling companion rather than an equal in office.

Chrysostom gives reasons for the choice of Cyprus and then withdraws them, since one may not ask why and wherefore when the Spirit is directing, and notes that preaching to the Jews first avoided making them more contentious. Cyril recounts the whole Antioch chain, from Barnabas fetching Paul out of Tarsus to the naming of Christians and the Spirit's command.

debates: Whether the reason for choosing Cyprus may be sought at all: Chrysostom lists reasons and then forbids the question, since the Spirit was directing, while Henry and Robertson ground the choice in Barnabas's birth on the island

What John Mark's office was: help in the actual preaching (Calvin), the synagogue attendant's role and perhaps baptising (Robertson, Ellicott), or minor offices and travel arrangements freeing the apostles for doctrine (Barnes, Clarke)
outliers: Calvin answers the charge that the apostles began amiss by preaching to Jews, arguing that the new commission to the Gentiles did not depose them from the office they already held

6.pericope_label: Paphos, the proconsul, and Elymas the sorcerer

schools.summary: Gill supplies the antiquities of Paphos and holds that Elymas interprets the name Bar-jesus rather than the word for sorcerer. Calvin refuses to read Luke's silence about the journey as failure, marvels that the gospel should reach so foul a place, reads the proconsul's superstition as a search for something better than his childhood religion, and turns the sorcerer's opposition into a warning about the enticements Satan supplies where no magician is present.

Lightfoot examines whether the second element of Bar-jesus is a proper name or a common noun, reports the Syriac reading of it as son of a swelling or a wound, and concludes that Elymas cannot interpret the name at all if it is a proper name.

Clarke states the rule distinguishing imperial from senatorial provinces, calls Paphos perhaps the most dissolute town in the world, insists that Elymas glosses the word for sorcerer, and speculates that the proconsul's conversion is why his name vanished from the consular lists. Wesley notes that he was not overswayed by the sorcerer but wished to inquire further.

Robertson answers the old charge against Luke's use of 'proconsul' from the transfer of the province and from inscriptions naming proconsuls of Cyprus, one bearing the name Paulus. Ellicott recounts the same history with the coins of Claudius Barnes appeals to Lardner for the same vindication, reads the proconsul as candid and inquiring, and traces the sorcerer's resistance to threatened self-interest.

debates: Whether 'Elymas' interprets the title 'the sorcerer' (Barnes, Clarke, and Lightfoot by implication) or the name 'Bar-jesus' (Gill)

How the accuracy of 'proconsul' is to be defended: from the province's transfer to the Senate (Robertson, Clarke), from surviving coins and inscriptions (Ellicott, Robertson), or on the authority of earlier scholarship (Barnes)
outliers: Clarke conjectures that Sergius Paulus was struck out of the consular records precisely because he became a Christian
Robertson meets surprise that an intelligent governor kept a sorcerer by recalling Juvenal's picture of the emperor on Capri surrounded by his astrologers

9.pericope_label: Paul rebukes Elymas, and the proconsul believes

schools.summary: Gill explains the two names by ordinary Jewish custom. Calvin defends the severity as neither hasty nor personal, since Paul begins with doctrine and turns on the man only when he sees him openly fighting the gospel under the Spirit's guidance; he treats the punitive power as exceptional, rare because miracles should resemble a gentle Christ, and reads the proconsul's astonishment as reverence for doctrine, which is faith's beginning.

Lightfoot explains the double name from Paul's standing in both nations, compares Silas and Silvanus, and observes that Luke gives the Gentile name alone from the moment the apostle of the Gentiles begins his work among them.

Clarke derives the name from a Hebrew root meaning wonderful on Jerome's authority, insists that the prediction of a blindness not yet visible proves immediate inspiration, stresses that the penalty was temporary and merciful, reports the tradition that Elymas was afterwards converted, and calls the word a two-edged sword. Wesley divides the charges between the false prophet and the magician.

Ellicott connects the new name with the proconsul's conversion and lists three reasons for its adoption, traces the vocabulary of trickery, and suggests that Paul chose blindness in prayer out of memory of his own. Robertson denies that the name was new at all and dismisses the borrowing theory as vulgar, describes the rebuke as deadly accurate, and answers the objection that a proconsul could not be converted by a miracle. Barnes reports the Latin sense of the name and traces the vocabulary of trickery.
Cyril, expounding the power at work in the apostles, insists that the Spirit who fills them is one and undivided while his operations are various.

debates: Whether Paul took the name from Sergius Paulus at this moment (Ellicott, with Jerome) or had borne it from birth as a Roman citizen, the borrowing theory being beneath him (Robertson, Lightfoot, Gill)
What the name means: little or dwarfish from the Latin (Barnes) or wonderful from a Hebrew root (Clarke)
outliers: Calvin treats the apostolic power to punish as a deliberate rarity, since miracles ought for the most part to resemble the gentleness of Christ, and denies the apostles could use it at their own discretion
Robertson allows that Sergius Paulus may have believed without openly joining the Christians, no baptism being recorded, and denies that conversion need have cost him his office

13.pericope_label: From Paphos to Antioch of Pisidia, and John Mark turns back

schools.summary: Calvin names John Mark's withdrawal softness, explains that Luke records it because it later caused a sorry quarrel, and reads the praise of the others' constancy into the same sentence; on the sabbath assembly he distinguishes the figure now fulfilled in Christ from the practical use of a day set free for worship, which still holds. Gill traces the later history of a church at Perga through its martyrs and bishops to fill the silence of the narrative.

Henry accepts the silence about Perga as ordinary selection, since the apostles' travels, like Christ's, pass over much worth recording. Lightfoot notes that Strabo's list of Pisidian cities omits Antioch, and observes that sitting down was the recognised posture of a teacher, so the rulers could infer that these visitors were preachers.

Clarke marks the reversal by which Paul is named before Barnabas from this point, guesses that Mark went to see his mother and Peter, supposes a long river passage up to Perga, and notes how many towns bore the name Antioch. Wesley ascribes the withdrawal to fatigue or fear and distinguishes this Antioch from the sending church.

Robertson explains the Greek idiom for a leader and his followers, quotes the tribute to Barnabas for accepting second place, suspects Mark resented the change of leadership, reports the conjectures of malaria and summer heat behind the sudden move inland, and identifies Antioch as a Roman colony really in Phrygia. Ellicott explains the silence about Perga by the absence of synagogues, supplies the city's foundation and status, and reads the sitting down as taking the rabbi's seat. Barnes distinguishes the province from the label and conjectures fear as Mark's motive.

debates: Why John Mark turned back: fear of the journey (Barnes, Wesley), family ties at Jerusalem (Clarke, Ellicott), resentment at Paul's new leadership (Robertson), or plain softness (Calvin)
Why nothing is recorded of Perga: because there was no synagogue to preach in (Ellicott), or because the narrative simply passes over much that happened (Henry)
outliers: Clarke places Perga a long way up the river Cestrus while Ellicott puts it only seven miles from the mouth, a discrepancy neither notices
Barnes and Robertson agree that Antioch lay in Phrygia and was called Pisidian only to distinguish it from the Antioch in Syria

15.pericope_label: The invitation to speak, and the opening of Paul’s sermon

schools.summary: Gill counts the annual cycle of the law and takes Paul's rising as acceptance of the invitation. Calvin draws a rule of worship from the order described, the Scriptures holding the first place because nothing may be set before the Church that is not drawn from them and exposition coming second, and notes that all alike were admitted to the reading; he also states the root of Paul's argument, that Israel's whole privilege hung on the promise of a Saviour.
Lightfoot questions whether the Greek Bible could have been understood in Pisidia at all, citing Strabo's list of four regional languages in which Pisidian is distinguished from Greek.

Clarke supplies the tables of law and prophet lessons, presses the same difficulty about language, and praises Paul for proving his case by plain history rather than rhetorical art. Wesley supposes the apostles asked leave to speak beforehand as a matter of decency, and takes those who feared God to be proselytes or heathens indifferently.

Ellicott dates the lectionary, uses the echoes of the day's two lessons to fix the very sabbath of the sermon, is certain that Paul spoke Greek throughout, and reads the hand gesture as a call for silence reported by an eyewitness. Barnes describes the rulers' powers and admires Paul's postponement of his main claim. Robertson supplies the history of the readings and sees in the God-fearers the opening Paul needed to the pagan world.

Chrysostom notes Barnabas giving place to the man he had fetched from Tarsus, as John gave way to Peter, both looking only to the common advantage; and he observes that Paul praises his hearers before arguing with them, avoiding the word proselytes as a term of disadvantage.

debates: Whether the Scriptures could have been read and the sermon preached in Greek at Antioch: Lightfoot and Clarke doubt it from Strabo's account of the Pisidian languages, while Ellicott calls it absolutely certain from the verbal echoes of the day's lessons
Whether standing to speak was the Jewish custom (Chrysostom) or the Greek and Roman one, the Jewish being to sit (Robertson)
outliers: Ellicott identifies the exact sabbath of the sermon from the two appointed lessons, both of which Paul quotes, and concludes that he began from what the congregation had just heard read

17.pericope_label: From the choosing of the fathers to the raising up of David

schools.summary: Gill lists the seven nations and the judges by name. Calvin reads the whole preface as proof that Paul brought in nothing new, keeps the harsher reading by which God bore with a stubborn people, and takes the commendation of David not as praise of the man but as a device for lifting the hearers' minds to the Christ whom David figured, the mention of Jesse enlarging the grace.

Lightfoot argues from the qualifying word 'about' that the forty years may cover the span between the decree of exclusion and the entry into Canaan, and notes with Clarke that 'the seven nations' was a fixed rabbinic term.

Clarke reports Scaliger's name for the chronological crux, treats the two readings of the disputed verb as of equal value, and restricts the praise of David, on Benson's authority, to his public conduct as a ruler. Wesley calls these verses the sum of the Old Testament, includes Samuel's years in Saul's forty, and warns that taking 'a man after God's own heart' for David's whole character is a gross and dangerous mistake.

Ellicott identifies Stephen's plan behind the speech, prefers the reading that makes God nurse rather than endure his people, and resolves the four hundred and fifty years by a better text that attaches them to what precedes. Robertson concurs on both readings and on the composite quotation about David. Barnes states the chronological difficulty against the figure in Kings and canvasses the proposed solutions.

debates: Whether the disputed verb means that God bore with Israel's manners (Barnes, Calvin) or nursed them as a father carries his child (Ellicott, Robertson), Clarke calling the readings of equal value

How the four hundred and fifty years are to be reckoned: as the period of the judges, requiring a chronological solution (Barnes, Clarke), or as the interval before them on a better reading (Ellicott, Robertson)
What 'a man after mine own heart' commends: David's public administration only (Clarke, Wesley) or the figure of Christ in him (Calvin)
outliers: Wesley states flatly that in the matter of Uriah David was as far from being a man after God's own heart as Saul was, and calls the contrary supposition dangerous
Robertson observes that Paul names his own tribe with pride while passing over Saul's sin in silence

23.pericope_label: The promised Saviour, the witness of John, and the ignorance of Jerusalem

schools.summary: Gill observes the Jewish claim on the title 'men', which they denied to the nations. Calvin grounds the mission in God's bare faithfulness to his own promise, explains why the Baptist's testimony carries weight, treats his question as rebuke rather than doubt, and shows how the objection from Jerusalem's authority could have overthrown the whole sermon had it not been met.

Clarke would render the address simply 'brethren', and calls the plea of ignorance a gentle excuse for the priests which nevertheless convicts them of not wishing to know God's will. Wesley argues that the Baptist's fame must have reached Pisidia, and finds in the condemnation of an innocent man the proof that the rulers had not understood their own prophets.

Robertson notes that the Baptist is asked what rather than who he is, and holds that ignorance mitigated the rulers' guilt without removing it. Ellicott judges that the names of Jesus and John were already vaguely known in Pisidia, contrasts the two classes in the audience, and turns the synagogue lectionary into a witness against the hearers at Jerusalem. Barnes admires the tenderness with which the murderers are described and keeps the word of salvation addressed particularly to Jews.

Cyril, marvelling at the same preacher, calls it a wise dispensation of the Spirit that the former persecutor was granted more epistles than the rest, so that the doctrine might stand beyond question.

debates: To whom the word of salvation is said to be sent: to both Jews and God-fearers together as one audience (Robertson) or particularly to the Jewish people (Barnes)

How far the ignorance of the rulers excuses them: it is a gentle excuse that still convicts them of unwillingness to know (Clarke), a mitigation of degree only (Robertson), or a charge proved by their own sentence on an innocent man (Wesley)
outliers: Ellicott infers from the frequency of pilgrimage that the story of Jesus and of John was already vaguely known in Pisidia, so that Paul speaks as one offering clearness rather than news
Calvin explains that Christ's death at Jerusalem was itself the strongest objection to the gospel, since to receive one cast out of the temple looked like departing from the Church

28.pericope_label: The death of the guiltless, the raising up, and the second psalm

schools.summary: Gill notes that the suborned witnesses could not support their charges and that Pilate declared the innocence repeatedly. Calvin grounds the doctrine of justification on that innocence, since a death suffered for a man's own crimes could not satisfy for others; admits the difficulty in saying that the killers buried him, makes the resurrection the ground on which the death can be preached at all, and uses the word 'children' to defend a natural posterity against allegorising interpreters.

Henry makes the resurrection the great proof of Christ's sonship, since one who had life in himself could not be held by death. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic discussion bearing on whether the psalm beginning 'why do the heathen rage' was counted separately from the first.

Clarke argues that God would not raise the dead except on an extraordinary occasion so that the rising proves the innocence, and canvasses the manuscript evidence for 'the first psalm' while rejecting it. Wesley insists that Christ was Son of God from eternity, so that the begetting is a declaration, beautifully dated from the day he seemed born out of the earth anew.

Barnes describes the legal manoeuvre, answers the difficulty about the burial, and takes the sonship in the psalm to be declared by the resurrection. Ellicott traces the shifting accusations, hears in the account of the witnesses a man who had questioned them himself, and prefers the reading 'unto our children'. Robertson notes that Paul knew the innocence before any Gospel was written, treats the variants as a primitive corruption, and distinguishes the raising up of this verse from the resurrection.
Cyril turns the words of the second psalm against those who confess one God but deny that he is the Father of Jesus Christ, and so set themselves against their own prophets.

debates: What 'this day have I begotten thee' asserts: a sonship constituted or evidenced by the resurrection (Barnes, Henry) or an eternal sonship publicly declared on that day (Wesley)
Whether the 'raising up' of the quotation refers to the resurrection at all, Robertson distinguishing it as the sending of Jesus and finding two different raisings in the passage
How to read the reference to the second psalm, given manuscripts and Hebrew copies in which the first two psalms are one (Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, with Lightfoot's rabbinic evidence)
outliers: Calvin insists that 'children' means natural descendants, against interpreters who dissolve the promise into allegory and so empty the covenant made with Abraham's seed
Robertson observes that Paul could assert Christ's innocence though no Gospel had yet been written

34.pericope_label: No more to corruption: the sure mercies of David and the psalm David could not fulfil

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the raising up from the raising from the dead, records the variant renderings of the second citation, and describes David's service as government, protection and the promotion of worship. Calvin argues that a resurrection still liable to change would leave a cold hope, that the perpetuity of Christ's life is ours because he rose for our sake, and that the prophecy, fulfilled perfectly in Christ as head, holds also for the members in their measure.

Lightfoot observes that the phrase comes from the Greek of Isaiah, and that the rabbis themselves understood 'David' there of the Messiah, so that the sure mercies of David are properly the sure mercies of Christ.

Clarke takes corruption for the grave rather than putrefaction, and argues from David's undisturbed decay that the psalm can be applied to Jesus only. Wesley reads the sure mercies as blessings solid to every believer which require the resurrection, contrasts David's service to one generation with a ministry to all, and turns the verse into a direct question to the reader about whether he is serving God's will now.

Barnes and Robertson agree that corruption here means death or the grave, Robertson adding that Christ did not return like Lazarus. Ellicott concedes that the words from Isaiah are not in themselves messianic but become pregnant to a mind full of the prophets, and hears in David's ministry to one generation a contrast with the endless ministry of the Son of Man. Barnes calls the phrase about serving a generation almost unintelligible; Robertson finds three constructions all defensible.
Cyril quotes the psalm under a different number and applies its earlier verses to those who refused Christ and chose Caesar for their king before coming to the promise about corruption.

debates: How the promise of the sure mercies bears on the resurrection: because 'David' in the prophet already means the Messiah (Lightfoot, Clarke) or because words not in themselves messianic become so to minds steeped in prophecy (Ellicott), or because the blessings could not otherwise be given (Wesley)
How to construe the clause about serving one's own generation, which Barnes calls almost unintelligible and Robertson leaves open among three grammatical possibilities
outliers: Calvin extends the prophecy beyond its head, holding that what was fulfilled perfectly in Christ takes place in every member according to his measure
Cyril's citation of this psalm under a different number is a further witness to the variant psalm-numbering discussed at the previous verse

38.pericope_label: Forgiveness and justification proclaimed, with a warning from the prophets

schools.summary: Gill excludes works, evangelical obedience, inward holiness and even the grace of faith from the ground of justification, leaving only faith's object, and insists the acquittal covers every kind of sin. Calvin marks the turn from how salvation was purchased to what Christ's office brings, reads the passage as teaching justification by faith alone, explains the severity as a hammer for stubborn hearers that still leaves room for repentance, and shows how the altered wording of the prophet extends his threat to despisers in every age.
Henry makes justification exclusive to believers and states the sinner's whole concern in a sentence: if anything remains charged upon him he is undone.

Clarke lays the conclusion out as a chain of concessions from promise, failure, incorruption and fulfilled prophecy, prints the Hebrew and Greek of the closing citation beside Paul's abridgement, and observes how pointedly the threat was fulfilled in the fall of the city and temple. Wesley fixes forgiveness at the moment of believing, denies that the law ever could justify since it had no expiation for presumptuous sins, and warns that the familiar division of the law into moral and ceremonial is not in view here at all.

Ellicott presses the tense that makes forgiveness a present proclamation, renders the preposition as marking the sphere rather than the instrument, notes the forensic sense of the verb in this earliest specimen of Paul's teaching, and observes that the prophet quoted supplied the axiom of Paul's life. Robertson analyses the Greek period whose climax falls last, credits both 'despisers' and 'perish' to the Greek version, and guesses that Paul saw anger on the rabbis' faces. Barnes traces the citation to the Septuagint and thinks the caution needed because the Jews held themselves secure.

debates: Whether the law of Moses is here considered as a whole or only in part: Wesley denies that the familiar division into moral and ceremonial is in view, Moses and Christ being simply opposed, while Barnes reads the failure as belonging to the sacrificial system in particular

How the altered wording of the prophecy is to be justified: as the ordinary use of the Greek version (Barnes, Robertson, Ellicott) or as a deliberate widening that makes the ancient threat reach every despiser (Calvin)
outliers: Ellicott notes that this sermon contains the first recorded use by Paul of the word 'justified', already in the forensic sense that became characteristic of him
Wesley denies that the law ever could have justified, at any period, since it provided no expiation for presumptuous sins

42.pericope_label: The request for a second hearing, and those who followed the apostles

schools.summary: Gill notes the copies that omit the clause about the synagogue and asks whether the assembly was dismissed in order or broke up in disorder. Calvin prefers to read the phrase with the Jews, so that the apostles left while the assembly still sat, and is alone in stating plainly that the closing exhortation may run either way, the hearers urging constancy on the preachers or the preachers strengthening the hearers.

Henry explains the walkout as incensed refusal to hear preaching addressed to themselves rather than to the Gentiles, done by agreement and in contempt. Lightfoot argues that the Greek order favours the rendering by which the apostles besought the Gentiles, and that the departure of offended Jews makes it the likelier sense.

Clarke prefers the same rendering as Lightfoot and pictures the apostle turning to better-minded hearers, identifies the departing Jews with the despisers of the prophecy, takes the proselytes for proselytes of the gate, and glosses continuance in grace as crediting the gospel and bringing forth its fruits. Wesley thinks many left before the sermon ended, refers the appointed day to the sabbath between the first and tenth of Tisri, and gives the reason for the exhortation, that trials were at hand.

Ellicott and Robertson hold that the better manuscripts omit 'the Gentiles' altogether, Robertson adding that the received text wrongly makes the Jews hostile from the first when both parties asked for a repetition. Barnes surveys the manuscripts and versions and concludes the true reading may be undeterminable. Ellicott also settles the day as the following sabbath, notes that both classes followed, and supposes the apostles worked at their trade during the week.

Chrysostom traces the request for a second hearing to Paul's deliberate restraint: he dropped seeds and declined to resolve the questions he had raised, stating the fact of remission without explaining how, so as to leave his hearers wanting more rather than sated.

debates: Whether the Gentiles besought the apostles or the apostles besought the Gentiles (Lightfoot and Clarke preferring the latter on the order of the words), or whether the word 'Gentiles' belongs in the text at all (Ellicott, Robertson), with Barnes judging the reading undeterminable
Who exhorts whom to continue in the grace of God, Calvin allowing that the hearers may be urging constancy on the preachers as readily as the reverse
outliers: Wesley identifies the appointed day with the sabbath falling between the first and tenth of Tisri, which sits awkwardly beside Ellicott's earlier dating of the sermon to the forty-fourth sabbath of the year
Ellicott infers from the apostles' trade that they supported themselves by tent-making during the intervening week

44.pericope_label: Almost the whole city, the envy of the Jews, and the turn to the Gentiles

schools.summary: Gill refers the command not to the prophet but to the enlarged commission given after the resurrection. Calvin takes the crowd as proof of unwearied work between the sabbaths while suspecting the hearers were still undecided, states as a rule that the wicked rage more as the light comes nearer, reads the rebuke as a deliberate excommunication reserved for the hopeless, and holds that the prophet's words are addressed to the Son though much that Scripture gives Christ belongs to his ministers as well.

Clarke argues that conversion comes as much through the private conduct of believers scattered like leaven as through public preaching, and turns their use of Scripture into a rule that no minister should go farther than he can say it is written, with quotations fairly made. Wesley says hinderers must be publicly reproved, catches the irony that men who thought none but themselves worthy pronounced themselves unworthy by refusing, and denies that the turn to the Gentiles ended preaching to Jews elsewhere.

Ellicott shows that the synagogue could not have held the crowd and offers two arrangements for it, explains the envy as outrage at seeing Gentiles treated as brethren on the same level rather than as tolerated inferiors, and calls the citation the germ of the argument later developed in Romans. Robertson distinguishes these Jews from the proselytes of the previous verse and blames the rabbis, noting that no such crowds came for them. Barnes explains the word for envy and accounts for the appeal to the Old Testament rather than to the words of Jesus.

debates: To whom the words of the prophet are addressed: to the Son, with only a derived application to his ministers (Calvin, Wesley), or to the apostles as their commission (Gill, and the sense Robertson gives the command)
Whether the prophet's words constitute a commission that may be transferred to preachers at all, Calvin conceding much to Christ's ministers while reserving titles proper to his person
outliers: Clarke lays down that a preacher must go no farther than he can say 'it is written', and must not produce a detached clause because it happens to suit the system he wishes to establish
Barnes explains the appeal to Isaiah rather than to Christ's own command by the fact that the hearers acknowledged the prophets but would have scorned a word of Jesus of Nazareth

48.pericope_label: The Gentiles rejoice, the word spreads, and the apostles are driven out

schools.summary: Gill takes the honourable women for wealthy Gentile proselytes, traces the later church of the region, and asks whether the disciples filled with joy are the apostles or the converts. Calvin makes the Gentiles' gladness rest on finding their calling long foretold rather than sudden, sees the parable of the leaven fulfilled in the spread, defends the shaking of the dust as a sign already known to be a curse, and prefers to read the closing joy as the reign of the Spirit's grace.

Clarke denies that the participle rendered 'ordained' contains any idea of pre-ordination, since neither compound that would say so is used; he explains the dust-shaking as a declaration that the land itself was accursed, and closes with the observation that a Christian's happiness lies beyond the reach of earthly disturbance, the martyrs being happier in the flames than their persecutors on beds of down. Wesley argues from the time rather than the grammar, that the ordination described took place at the very hour of hearing.

Ellicott renders the disputed clause 'as many as were disposed for eternal life' and suspects the English word was coloured by the theology current when the version was made; he infers a long period of work from the spread of the word, explains how proselytising bore on the women who were stirred up, and reverses the symbolism of the dust so that the unbelieving Jews are the unclean. Robertson notes the Jews' small numbers but wide influence, and recalls that the blood of the martyrs is still the seed of the church. Barnes reports the ancient versions of the disputed clause and finds in the joy a proof that the gospel holds in the severest trials.
Cyril, expounding the same gladness, sets beside it the apostolic charge to rejoice in the Lord always, since redemption has drawn near.

debates: What 'ordained to eternal life' asserts: an eternal decree (the sense the ancient versions carry, reported by Barnes), a disposition or fitness (Ellicott), an appointment made at the moment of hearing (Wesley), or nothing about pre-ordination at all, on the form of the participle (Clarke)
Whether the shaking of the dust was an invented sign or an existing Jewish token of cursing, Calvin arguing that Christ would not have prescribed a gesture nobody understood
outliers: Ellicott suspects that the translators' choice of the word 'ordained' was itself shaped by the theology prevailing in the English Church when the version was made

Ellicott pictures the effect of the mission concretely: in every town of the region a few men and women who had stopped sacrificing to their country's gods and would not be confined to the synagogue either
